All three national names are late. Rübenczal is on the map in 1561 and the German material is collected from 1662. Krakonoš is Klicpera's, from 1824. Liczyrzepa translates the German. Mateusz J. Hartwich has documented how the teacher Józef Sykulski, who settled in Hirschberg in 1945, set out to make the mountain spirit a Pole. The figure three countries argue over was assembled in print between 1662 and 1824.

fate: No death: still rules the Giant Mountains under different names.

chain.claim: Rübezahl is an ancient Germanic mountain god, a pre-Christian deity of the Giant Mountains who survived Christianisation as a folk spirit.
chain.verdict: The documents on this ladder run back to the sixteenth century, where Rübezahl appears as a named mountain demon rather than as a god, and in the places where an ancient-deity reading is stated it is stated as conjecture.

rungs.witness: Łukasz Kozak, Vom Berggeist zu Gandalf, Goethe-Institut magazine
rungs.date: September 2018
rungs.reads: Reports that some people see in Rübezahl a late echo of the veneration of Scandinavian and Germanic gods such as Odin, Heimdall or Thor, and immediately frames this as one opinion among several while saying the origin remains unknown. This is the claim in circulation, presented as opinion rather than as documented.
rungs.evidence: https://www.goethe.de/ins/cz/de/kul/the/erb/21339184.html, article by Łukasz Kozak, September 2018. It contains the sentence "Manche meinen, in Rübezahl einen späten Nachhall der Verehrung skandinavischer und germanischer Götter zu erkennen", continuing with Odin, Heimdall and Thor as the examples. It describes the Helwig map figure at the foot of the Schneekoppe, and states that the origin is unknown.
rungs.note: The same article cites Jan Długosz on the year 1367, but that passage concerns Bytom mine owners murdering two clergymen, not the mountain spirit.

rungs.witness: Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache, Herkunft von Rübezahl, Der Sprachdienst 6/2009, Fragen und Antworten
rungs.reads: States that there is still no secure explanation of the name, that Praetorius in 1662 already ran through more than a dozen designations without settling it, and that the turnip-counting story is a later folk etymology rather than the source of the name. Silent on any Germanic deity.
rungs.evidence: https://gfds.de/ruebezahl/, published by the Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache in Der Sprachdienst 6/2009 under Fragen und Antworten. It says no secure explanation of the name exists, cites Praetorius 1662 and his dozen-plus designations, notes a medieval surname possibly meaning turnip tail, and makes no mention of a pre-Christian or Germanic deity.

rungs.witness: Johann Karl August Musäus, Volksmährchen der Deutschen, Zweyter Theil, containing the Legenden von Rübezahl, Gotha, C. W. Ettinger
rungs.reads: Five literary legends. Rübezahl is a Berggeist, a mountain spirit, and the name is explained inside the fiction as a mocking nickname earned by counting turnips. The book supplies the etymology that later readers take for tradition, and it supplies no deity.
rungs.evidence: https://archive.org/details/legenden_ruebezahl_volksmaerchen_22_librivox describes the source text as Volksmärchen der Deutschen, Zweiter Theil, containing the Legenden von Rübezahl, 1783, and counts five legends about the Berggeist. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volksm%C3%A4rchen_der_Deutschen gives the volume years as 1782, 1783, 1784, 1786 and 1787, published by C. W. Ettinger in Gotha. https://gfds.de/ruebezahl/ attributes the turnip-counting nickname to Musäus and says it is offered with a wink rather than as an etymology.
rungs.note: The English Wikipedia article body places the Rübezahl legends in volume 1, which conflicts with the 1783 second volume named on the archive.org record. The catalogue entry's 1783 date is supported.

rungs.witness: Johannes Praetorius, Daemonologia Rubinzalii Silesii, three parts
rungs.date: 1662 to 1673; digitised original copy at the Thüringer Universitäts- und Landesbibliothek Jena, shelfmark HZ: 12 Bud.Jus publ.84(2)
rungs.reads: The largest early corpus of Rübezahl material. Its own title page calls the subject a Gespenst, a spectre, described as very old and widely reported, which shows itself to travellers in the mountains of Silesia and Bohemia. It reports a haunting, not a deity with worship.
rungs.evidence: https://collections.thulb.uni-jena.de/receive/HisBest_cbu_00021972 gives the title as "Daemonologia Rubinzalii silesii. Das ist/ Ein ausführlicher Bericht/ Von den wunderbarlichen/ sehr Alten/ und weit-beschrienen Gespenste Dem Rübezahl : Welches sich/ auf den Gebirgen in Schlesien und Böhmen/ den Wanders-Leuten zum öfftern ... erzeiget", author M. Johannes Praetorius, imprints Leipzig, Arnstadt and Rudolstadt, dates 1662 to 1673, holding library ThULB Jena, shelfmark HZ: 12 Bud.Jus publ.84(2). https://books.google.com/books?id=GqFQAAAAcAAJ shows a 1662 printing of the same work.
rungs.note: The imprint spans Leipzig, Arnstadt and Rudolstadt and the dates run to 1673, wider than the Leipzig 1662 to 1665 given in the catalogue entry.

rungs.witness: Martin Helwig, Silesiae Typus, woodcut map of Silesia, cut by H. Kron of Breslau and printed by Johannes Creutziger in Neisse
rungs.date: printed 1561; sole surviving copy of the first edition in the Badische Landesbibliothek Karlsruhe
rungs.reads: Carries an upright figure at the foot of the Riesengebirge with antlers, goat feet, a tail and a branch, labelled Rübenczal. It attests the name and a demonic image in Silesian print by 1561. It gives the figure no divine title, no cult, no worshippers and no antiquity.
rungs.evidence: http://www.spata-bonn.de/heltext.pdf, a text on the 1561 Helwig map, describes the figure as an upright walking creature at the foot of the Riesengebirge with stag's antlers, goat feet, a tail and a branch, calls it the earliest depiction of the legendary figure, gives the map label as Rübenczal, and places the original in the Badische Landesbibliothek Karlsruhe. https://www.hausschlesien.de/ausstellungen/253-die-mutter-aller-andern-schlesischen-landcharten states that the only surviving copy of the 1561 first edition is in the Badische Landesbibliothek Karlsruhe and that eleven editions appeared down to 1889. https://www.vermessungsgeschichte.de/detail/schlesienkarte-von-1561 names Kron as the woodcutter and Creutziger in Neisse as the printer and confirms the Karlsruhe copy. https://dewiki.de/Lexikon/R%C3%BCbezahl (mirror of German Wikipedia) describes the same figure as a tailed demon among mountains and villages.
rungs.note: The English Wikipedia article on Helwig reports that the Wrocław copy of the 1561 map was lost in the war, which is consistent with a single survivor elsewhere.

chain.floor: A printed map of 1561 puts a named, horned, goat-footed and tailed mountain demon into Silesian print, and a 1662 compilation calls the same figure a spectre. The documents assembled here begin in the sixteenth century and describe a haunting: a god, a cult, worshippers or a pre-Christian date are not among the things they supply.

name: Giant of Kandahar
shortDescription: Unverified modern military legend of a red-haired giant near Kandahar.
fullDescription: The Giant of Kandahar is a story that a US special forces team killed a red-haired, six-fingered giant in Afghanistan in 2002. There is no evidence for it, and the story's actual history is documentable.
mysteryNote: War makes large shadows. Not every shadow has a body that a laboratory has held, or that paperwork admits.
sources: Paranormal radio and internet forum circulation, mid-2000s onward
Cable television treatments, 2010s (amplification, not evidence)
Absence of corroborating US military records; reported FOIA results
Comparative: 19th-c. American giant lore and Nephilim literature

sections.story:
The claim, as it circulates, is specific enough to sound like a report. A US special operations patrol goes missing in Kandahar province. A second team is sent, finds a cave, and encounters a giant: variously twelve to fifteen feet tall, red-haired, with six fingers on each hand and two rows of teeth. It kills one soldier with a spear before being shot. The body is flown out and everything is classified.

None of this is supported by anything.

What can be traced is where the story came from. It surfaced through paranormal talk radio and internet forums in the 2000s, gained wide circulation through repetition, and was substantially amplified by cable television treatments in the 2010s. The named witnesses are anonymous or unverifiable. No unit, no date, no casualty record, and no serviceman has ever been identified. US military casualties in Afghanistan are documented in detail, and no death matches the account.

The physical details are worth noticing because they are not random. Red hair, six fingers and double rows of teeth are the standard inventory of nineteenth-century American giant lore and of the Nephilim literature: the same features attached to the Lovelock Cave claims elsewhere in this codex. The Kandahar story is assembled from an existing kit.

Its persistence is the genuinely interesting part: a war zone that is closed to verification, a claim of classification that makes absence of evidence into evidence, and an audience for whom the giants of Genesis are a live proposition.

We include it because the codex covers modern legend, and this is a clean specimen of one forming in traceable conditions. It is not a report of an event.
sections.origins:
The story has no primary source. Its documented history runs through paranormal radio programming and internet forums from the mid-2000s onward.

Cable television treatments, particularly in the 2010s, gave it mass circulation and are the route by which most people encountered it.

No military record, casualty report, unit history or named participant supports it. Freedom of Information requests reported by journalists have produced nothing.

Its component details derive from a long tradition of American giant lore and from Nephilim literature, both of which are documented and considerably older.
sections.disputed:
There is nothing to dispute in the ordinary sense. No evidence has been produced in more than two decades.

The classification claim is unfalsifiable by design, and that is a recognised feature of this kind of story rather than an argument in its favour.

What is genuinely worth studying is the transmission: how a claim with no source acquires circumstantial detail, named-sounding witnesses and television airtime. The Kandahar story is unusually well documented as a case of that process because it happened recently and online.

Treating this entry as evidence of anything other than how modern legends form would be a misreading of it.

fate: No verified fate: the claim has no primary source at all.

chain.claim: In 2002 a US special forces patrol in the mountains of Kandahar province, Afghanistan, was attacked by a giant twelve to thirteen feet tall, red-haired, with six fingers on each hand and two rows of teeth. It killed one American with a spear before the team shot it. The body was recovered, flown out of the country, and the incident was classified.
chain.verdict: The story is carried by datable broadcasts, articles and podcasts rather than by any record of an event, and the tellings on this ladder contradict one another about where the body went, when the sighting happened and who was present, while the published casualty accounting and the replies given to journalists hold nothing matching the account.

rungs.witness: MrBallen Podcast: Strange, Dark & Mysterious Stories, episode "The Cemetery/Kandahar Giant | Campfire Stories with MrBallen" (transcript)
rungs.date: Released 24 April 2026, running time about 50 minutes
rungs.reads: The fully developed narrative, in the version most listeners now meet. The transcript has "In 2002, there was this Army infantry unit that was out doing a patrol in the Kandahar mountain range", places Mr K among Green Berets, has a spear impale a soldier called Dan in plain view of the others, and on the body says that a second helicopter "had this huge net that they basically wrapped around this dead huge giant, and they strapped it up to the underside of the helo, and then they flew off with this giant". Every element the claim needs is present here, and none of it is present in the 2005 telling.
rungs.evidence: Transcript at https://podcasts.happyscribe.com/mrballen-podcast-strange-dark-mysterious-stories/kandahar-giant-campfire-stories-with-mrballen fetched twice this session with different prompts; both returns reproduced the three quoted passages, and the page showed the episode as published three months before 8 August 2026. The exact release date of 24 April 2026 and the 50 minute duration were taken from the Spotify episode page https://open.spotify.com/episode/5yLHQprlAJLYTKil8TdMEL fetched this session.
rungs.note: A retelling, not a source. Its value on the ladder is that it lets the 2026 shape of the story be set beside the 2005 shape and compared item by item.

rungs.witness: United States Department of Defense, "CASUALTY STATUS" summary sheet (war.gov/casualty.pdf)
rungs.date: Figures given as of 10 a.m. EST, 30 January 2025
rungs.reads: The official running tally for Operation Enduring Freedom. For Afghanistan only it gives 2,219 total deaths, 1,833 hostile, 385 non-hostile and 1 pending, with 20,093 wounded in action. It says nothing about the claim, and that is its use: it shows that American deaths in Afghanistan are counted individually and sorted by cause, so a death of the kind the story asserts would have a place in a public schedule of this sort.
rungs.evidence: https://www.war.gov/casualty.pdf fetched twice this session with different prompts. Both returns gave the as-of line for 10 a.m. EST, Jan. 30, 2025, and the same Afghanistan-only row: 2,219 total, 1,833 hostile, 385 non-hostile, 1 pending, 20,093 WIA.
rungs.note: This is a summary sheet of totals, not a name-by-name list, so it cannot by itself exclude a particular death. It establishes that the accounting exists and is published.

rungs.witness: "Colossal: Fallen Angels and the Giant of Kandahar", documentary film directed by Clive Christopher
rungs.date: Release date 25 February 2025, running time 61 minutes
rungs.reads: A feature-length treatment built entirely around the claim. Its own synopsis presents the Kandahar giant as a creature encountered by US military personnel in Afghanistan and connects it to fallen angels and their reputed descendants. It offers the story as the subject of a documentary rather than as anything newly evidenced.
rungs.evidence: https://watch.plex.tv/movie/colossal-fallen-angels-and-the-giant-of-kandahar fetched this session, giving the title, the 25 February 2025 release date, the director Clive Christopher, the 61 minute running time, the cast entry for Stephen Campbell, and the synopsis paraphrased above. The film's existence and 2025 date were separately visible in search results for the IMDb entry tt35302102 and an Amazon Prime Video listing.
rungs.note: I have not watched the film. What is verified is that it exists under that title with that release date and that its published synopsis is about this claim.

rungs.witness: Bernadette Giacomazzo, "The Real Story Of The Kandahar Giant", All That's Interesting
rungs.date: Published 4 September 2023, page carrying a last-updated date of 14 July 2026
rungs.reads: This is where the 2016 layer is documented. It reports that the story reached the public through a video first posted on 16 August 2016 in which L. A. Marzulli interviewed an anonymous man identified only as Mr K, and states that the video has since been deleted. It reports that in August 2016 Snopes put the matter to the Department of Defense, which replied that it had "no record or information about a special forces member killed by a giant in Kandahar". It identifies nothing earlier than 2016 as a public telling of the specifically Kandahar version.
rungs.evidence: https://allthatsinteresting.com/kandahar-giant fetched twice this session with different prompts. Both returns gave the byline Bernadette Giacomazzo and the dates, and both reproduced, character for character, the sentence beginning "In a now-deleted video first posted on August 16, 2016" and the Department of Defense sentence quoted above.
rungs.note: The Department of Defense wording here is at two removes: a 2023 article quoting a 2016 fact-check quoting a departmental reply. I could not open the Snopes page itself, so this quotation is reported, not read at source.

rungs.witness: Nick Orton, "ENEMY UNKNOWN: High Strangeness in the Shadow of the Afghan War", The Havok Journal
rungs.date: Article carries two printed dates: an original publication date of 26 October 2022 and a republication date of 31 October 2025.
rungs.reads: A veterans' outlet setting out the story in the form it now circulates: it says the account was "A story made famous on Art Bell's Coast to Coast: AM", and describes it as revolving around a "special force" team meeting a giant redheaded man "with six fingers on each hand and double rows of teeth". Orton adds in the same sentence that these details are shared by many stories and accounts of giants from dozens of cultures in history. The article does not say a body was recovered or flown out.
rungs.evidence: https://havokjournal.com/culture/military/enemy-unknown-high-strangeness-in-the-shadow-of-the-afghan-war/ fetched twice this session with different prompts. Both returns gave the byline Nick Orton, both dates, and both reproduced the two quoted sentences identically. Both returns also stated that no passage in the article mentions a body being recovered or transported.
rungs.note: The Art Bell attribution is wrong: the 2005 show page names George Noory as host. The error is repeated in the Military Times piece below, which is itself evidence of how this story is transmitted.

rungs.witness: Geoff Ziezulewicz and J. D. Simkins, "Giants of Kandahar: outlandish tales of the US military in Afghanistan", Military Times
rungs.date: 1 November 2022
rungs.reads: A military trade paper treating the story as folklore. It reports that promoters of the story prompted the fact-checking outlet Snopes to investigate in 2016, and that "bewildered Pentagon officials told Snopes they had no record of such an incident". It attributes the story's mainstream reach to Coast to Coast AM and traces its recent circulation to Nick Orton's collection of military paranormal accounts.
rungs.evidence: https://www.militarytimes.com/off-duty/military-culture/2022/11/01/here-be-giants-outlandish-tales-of-the-military-the-afghan-colossi/ fetched twice this session with different prompts. Both returns gave the byline Geoff Ziezulewicz and J.D. Simkins and the date Nov 1, 2022, and both reproduced the sentence containing "no record of such an incident" and the sentence attributing mainstream attention to Coast to Coast AM.
rungs.note: This is a report of what the Pentagon told a third party in 2016, not a document from the Pentagon.

rungs.witness: Coast to Coast AM, programme of Wednesday 3 December 2008, "Flashpoints & Giants", guests Steve Quayle and Catherine Austin Fitts, with an anonymous pilot (broadcaster's own show page)
rungs.date: Broadcast 3 December 2008. The object consulted is the show summary on the broadcaster's website.
rungs.reads: Here the anonymous airman appears as a guest rather than as a forwarded email. He says he transported a dead giant, shot by the military, while stationed in Afghanistan. The summary gives "12 feet tall, give or take", around 1,100 pounds, six fingers on each hand, and canvas footwear, and says his superiors told him the body was "transloaded back to a base in Ohio". The height and the six fingers of the modern claim are present. The destination has moved from Europe to Ohio, and the account still contains no Kandahar, no special forces team, no cave, no spear and no American casualty.
rungs.evidence: https://www.coasttocoastam.com/show/2008-12-03-show/ fetched twice this session with different prompts. Both returns gave the date line as Wednesday, December 3, 2008, the title "Flashpoints & Giants", the guests Steve Quayle and Catherine Austin Fitts, and both reproduced the phrases "12 feet tall, give or take" and "transloaded back to a base in Ohio", the six fingers, and the pilot's claim to have transported a dead giant shot by the military while stationed in Afghanistan.
rungs.note: Two Quayle tellings three years apart send the same body to two different continents. That is the single most useful thing on this ladder.

rungs.witness: Coast to Coast AM, programme of Monday 7 November 2005, "Giants: Evidence & Legend", host George Noory, guest Steve Quayle (broadcaster's own show page)
rungs.date: Broadcast 7 November 2005. The object consulted is the show summary published on the broadcaster's website, whose date of writing is not stated.
rungs.reads: Quayle relays an email he says he received from a US Air Force officer, describing a dead giant the officer observed in Afghanistan about eight months earlier, flown to a secret military base in Europe. The summary gives the weight as about 1100 lbs, the height as roughly twice a normal human, and says the body had "an unusual odor". On the claim as it now circulates the page is silent at every load-bearing point: no Kandahar, no special forces patrol, no cave, no spear, no dead American, no red hair, no six fingers, no classification. The sighting is placed about eight months before November 2005, not in 2002, and the body goes to Europe.
rungs.evidence: https://www.coasttocoastam.com/show/2005-11-07-show/ fetched twice this session with different prompts. Both returns gave the date line as Monday, November 7, 2005, the host as George Noory, the guest as Steve Quayle, and both reproduced the sentence about an email from a US Air Force officer concerning a dead giant observed in Afghanistan eight months ago and flown to a base in Europe, together with the 1100 lbs figure and the phrase "an unusual odor". The same summary sentence is reproduced, with the same opening words, on the Sasquatch Chronicles post https://sasquatchchronicles.com/steve-quayle-giant-of-afghanistan/ dated 2 July 2020, which is how I checked that the wording is not an artefact of one fetch.
rungs.note: I did not hear the broadcast. What I verified is that the broadcaster's own archive carries a show of that date and title with that content summary.

chain.floor: Working back through the surviving documents, the 2005 Coast to Coast AM show page leaves standing something much smaller than the claim: a second-hand email, from an unnamed US Air Force officer, relayed on air by Steve Quayle, saying a dead giant was seen in Afghanistan about eight months before November 2005 and flown to a base in Europe. There is no Kandahar in it, no 2002, no special forces patrol, no cave, no spear, no dead American and no red hair. The height and the six fingers arrive three years later, in the 2008 broadcast, where the same body is sent to Ohio instead. The cave, the Green Berets, the killed soldier and the sling-loaded helicopter belong to the 2016 layer and after.

name: Giant of Kunar
shortDescription: Unverified legend of a giant observed in Kunar Province.
fullDescription: A parallel Afghanistan story places a giant in the Kunar valley. Like the Kandahar version, it has no verifiable source, and the two accounts have merged in circulation.
mysteryNote: Two provinces. One pattern of rumor. Zero paperwork, and a codex that refuses to launder rumor as fact.
sources: Paranormal radio and internet forum circulation, mid-2000s onward
Cable television treatments, 2010s (amplification, not evidence)
Absence of corroborating military records

sections.story:
The Kunar story runs on the same lines as the Kandahar one: a remote valley, a cave, a patrol, an enormous being, casualties, a recovered body, classification.

In practice the two are frequently told as one. Details migrate between them (the red hair, the six fingers, the spear), and different retellings place the same events in different provinces. That instability is itself informative. A report has a location; a legend has a setting, and settings are interchangeable.

Kunar province is mountainous, remote, and was among the harder areas of the Afghan conflict. It is exactly the kind of place a story like this attaches to: difficult terrain, limited access, genuine danger, and a long history of outside forces failing to control it.

Everything said about the Kandahar version applies here. There is no unit, no date, no casualty, no witness who can be identified, and no document. The claim that the evidence is classified performs the same function of insulating the story from checking.

What makes the pair worth keeping in a codex like this one is that they show a legend in its formative phase. Most of the entries here reach us through centuries of transmission with the origins lost. These two are perhaps twenty years old, they formed in public on recorded media, and the process can be watched.

They are also a reminder of the disclaimer this site carries on every modern-legend entry: unverified oral tradition is not a weaker kind of fact. It is a different kind of thing.
sections.origins:
No primary source exists, and that is the finding rather than a gap in our research.

Circulation runs through the same paranormal radio and internet ecosystem as the Kandahar story, from the mid-2000s onward. The earliest traceable appearances are forum posts and call-in segments, neither of which cite anything, and each subsequent retelling cites the previous one.

Television treatments in the 2010s carried both versions, frequently without distinguishing them, and are responsible for most of the story's present reach. Broadcast is not corroboration, though it is regularly mistaken for it.

No military documentation, casualty record, unit history or identifiable witness exists for either version. US deaths in Afghanistan are individually documented and none matches.

The two stories have substantially merged in retelling, and many accounts cannot now be assigned to one or the other.
sections.disputed:
Whether Kunar and Kandahar were ever distinct stories is unclear. They may have separate origins that converged, or one may be a relocated version of the other.

As with Kandahar, there is no evidence to weigh. The appropriate description is not "unproven" but "unsourced".

The value of the entry is documentary: it records that these claims exist and how they spread, not that anything happened.

Readers encountering confident retellings with specific details should note that specificity in this material tends to increase with distance from any source, which is the reverse of how evidence behaves.

fate: No verified fate: the claim has no primary source at all.

chain.claim: US forces operating in the Kunar valley in Afghanistan killed a giant, took casualties doing it, recovered the body, and the evidence was classified and suppressed.
chain.verdict: The documents that place a giant in Kunar describe something watched at a distance through a thermal sight, with no body and no classification, while the killing and the suppressed evidence attach to the Kandahar telling of the story.

rungs.witness: Greg Chabot, The Deadly Giants of Afghanistan: Mystery Tales From the GWOT, Soldier of Fortune
rungs.date: 27 October 2025
rungs.reads: Retells the Kunar episode as a 2008 sighting from an observation post through a prototype thermal scope, of a heat signature first taken for a group of fighters round a fire, which rose and walked away, estimated at 12 to 15 feet. Again nothing is killed and no body is recovered. The author states that he could find no official records for any of these Afghan giant accounts.
rungs.note: Soldier of Fortune is a commercial magazine sympathetic to this material, so its willingness to say the records are absent is worth recording. Its witnesses are anonymous.
rungs.evidence: https://sofmag.com/giants-of-afghanistan-gwot/ fetched this session. It gives the author as Greg Chabot and the date as 27 October 2025, and its Kunar paragraph describes a sighting from an observation post with no killing and no classification.

rungs.witness: Nick Orton, ENEMY UNKNOWN: High Strangeness in the Shadow of the Afghan War, The Havok Journal
rungs.date: 31 October 2025 for the version I read; Military Times cited a Havok Journal republication in 2022
rungs.reads: Carries the Kunar submission in fuller form, in the witness's own words as submitted anonymously. The observer watches the figure, then loses sight of it along a neighbouring spur and never sees it again. There is no killing, no body, no casualty and no mention of classified or suppressed evidence.
rungs.note: Compiled from anonymous submissions to the Tales From the Grid Square collection. The date given is the date of the version I fetched; the piece appears to be recirculated around Halloween, so an earlier posting of the same text is likely but I did not locate and date one.
rungs.evidence: https://havokjournal.com/culture/military/enemy-unknown-high-strangeness-in-the-shadow-of-the-afghan-war/ fetched this session. It gives Nick Orton as the byline and 31 October 2025 as the date, and carries the Kunar passage with the same tree sentence that appears in the 2022 Military Times article, confirming that the two are reproducing one account rather than two.

rungs.witness: Geoff Ziezulewicz and J. D. Simkins, Giants of Kandahar: outlandish tales of the US military in Afghanistan, Military Times
rungs.date: 1 November 2022
rungs.reads: This is the earliest dated item I could reach that names a Giant of Kunar. It describes a being an infantry team leader reportedly saw during a deployment between 2008 and 2009, through a newly mounted thermal sight, while overlooking a village at night: a large heat signature that stood up as one being. The account is of a sighting. Nothing is killed, no body is recovered, no unit or casualty is named, and no classification is claimed. The article attributes the account to Nick Orton's Tales From the Grid Square collection, and separately reports that Pentagon officials told Snopes they had no record of the Kandahar incident.
rungs.evidence: https://www.militarytimes.com/off-duty/military-culture/2022/11/01/here-be-giants-outlandish-tales-of-the-military-the-afghan-colossi/ fetched twice this session. It gives the two bylines and the date of 1 November 2022, carries the Giant of Kunar section, and quotes the witness saying 'The trees in that area grew up to about 10 to 12 ft tall, and this thing was at least as tall, if not taller than the trees that surrounded it.' A search for the exact phrase Giant of Kunar returned this article and its syndicated copies at Army Times, Marine Corps Times and Yahoo News, and no earlier use.

rungs.witness: L. A. Marzulli's video interview with a man identified only as Mr. K, posted to YouTube and since removed
rungs.date: posted 16 August 2016; the video is no longer available
rungs.reads: Reported by later writers as the item that put the killing into circulation: a 2002 cave encounter, a giant shot dead, US casualties, the body flown out, and the matter classified. The writers who summarise it place these events at Kandahar. Neither summary I read reports that it mentions Kunar.
rungs.note: This rung does not survive in a form I could consult. It rests on two secondary reports that agree on the date and on the fact of removal. I have not seen the video and make no claim about its exact wording.
rungs.evidence: https://allthatsinteresting.com/kandahar-giant and https://buttondown.com/Aborigen/archive/the-kandahar-giant/ both fetched this session. Both give 16 August 2016 for a Marzulli interview with a contractor called Mr. K, both describe the 2002 cave killing and the classification claim, and both state the video has been taken down. The Buttondown piece is dated 28 November 2023 and is a self-published newsletter.

rungs.witness: Above Top Secret forum thread 267559, titled Giant Cannibal Kills Troops In Afghanistan..???
rungs.date: thread started 11 February 2010; replies continue to 29 July 2016
rungs.reads: An anonymous internet discussion of a man-eating giant somewhere in Afghanistan. On the page I could read, no province is named, no giant is killed by US forces, and no classified or suppressed evidence is mentioned. Participants say they can find nothing online about the story and one replies that this is because it did not happen. It is therefore silent on Kunar and silent on the killing.
rungs.note: This is an unmoderated public forum, not journalism; I have classed it as press only because the schema offers no closer category. A poster on 12 April 2010 advertises his own book, Longwalkers: The Return of the Nephilim, and describes it as written in a fictional format, which is a fair indication of the register of the discussion.
rungs.evidence: https://www.abovetopsecret.com/forum/thread267559/pg2 fetched this session. The page carries the thread title, a thread start date of 11 February 2010, and dated posts of 11 February 2010, 10 and 12 April 2010, 23 and 26 July 2013 and 29 July 2016. Page 1 would not load: three attempts returned a robots.txt error, so I have not read the opening post and do not claim to know what it said.

chain.floor: The Kunar witness that can still be read is an anonymous account, published from 2022 onward and traced to a collection of reader submissions, of an infantry team leader who watched a large heat signature stand up on a ridge during a 2008 to 2009 deployment and then lost sight of it. It reports no body, no casualty, no unit and no classification. Talk of a giant and US troops in Afghanistan is attested in public discussion by February 2010, in a forum thread that names no province, cites no source, and has participants observing that nothing about it can be found. The cave, the killing and the classified evidence enter the record with a 2016 video interview about Kandahar that is no longer available to be checked. No document I reached this session places a killing in Kunar.

name: Paul Bunyan
height: As tall as the tale requires
shortDescription: Lumberjack giant of American tall tales: Babe the Blue Ox at his side.
fullDescription: Paul Bunyan is a giant lumberjack with a blue ox named Babe. He is the best-known giant in American folklore and substantially an advertising creation, which is the most interesting thing about him.
mysteryNote: The ox is blue because the winter was cold. Or because the story required it. On the frontier, that was evidence enough.
sources: Great Lakes logging-camp oral tradition, late 19th c.
James MacGillivray, Detroit News-Tribune (1910)
William Laughead, Red River Lumber Company pamphlets (1916 onward)
Richard Dorson, on fakelore (mid-20th c. critique)
imageAlt: Paul Bunyan and Babe the Blue Ox

sections.story:
The Paul Bunyan of popular knowledge scoops out the Great Lakes to water Babe, drags his axe behind him and gouges the Grand Canyon, and creates the ten thousand lakes of Minnesota with his and Babe's footprints. He clears forests at impossible speed. His griddle is greased by men skating across it with bacon strapped to their feet.

None of it asks to be believed. The tall tale is a genre with its own contract: the teller exaggerates, the listener knows, and the pleasure is in the escalation. This makes Bunyan structurally different from every other entry in this codex. He is not a belief that faded into story. He was a joke from the beginning.

His origins are genuinely in the logging camps of the Great Lakes region and eastern Canada, where oral tall tales about an outsized lumberjack circulated among workers in the later nineteenth century. That much is accepted.

What happened next is unusual. In 1916 the Red River Lumber Company, a California logging firm, began publishing promotional pamphlets written by an advertising man named William Laughead, featuring Paul Bunyan as a mascot. Laughead invented a great deal: Babe the Blue Ox appears to be substantially his, along with several of the supporting characters and much of the material now considered traditional.

The advertising Bunyan then escaped into general culture and became folklore in reverse: a commercial character absorbed into the national repertoire, taught in schools, and commemorated in enormous roadside statues across the northern United States.

Folklorists have argued about him for a century, with some calling the whole thing fakelore. He is a giant made of marketing that people genuinely adopted.
sections.origins:
Oral tall tales among lumber workers in the Great Lakes region and eastern Canada, later nineteenth century, are the genuine substrate. Documentation of this phase is thin.

Early print appearances include a 1910 newspaper piece by James MacGillivray in the Detroit News-Tribune.

William Laughead's promotional pamphlets for the Red River Lumber Company, from 1916 onward, are the decisive intervention and introduced much of the now-standard material including Babe.

Later literary treatments by Esther Shephard, James Stevens and others consolidated the figure. Richard Dorson's critique, coining the term fakelore, is the central scholarly intervention.
sections.disputed:
How much of Bunyan is authentically traditional and how much is Laughead's is the long-running argument. The oral substrate is accepted; its content is poorly documented, which makes the boundary hard to draw.

Richard Dorson's charge of fakelore has been influential and also contested. Critics argue that the distinction between authentic and commercial tradition is less clean than Dorson allowed, and that material genuinely adopted by a public is folklore whatever its origin.

Regional claims to Bunyan's origin (Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Maine, Quebec) are numerous, competitive and mostly commercially motivated.

Some early logging-camp material was rough and, by modern standards, offensive in ways later versions removed. The sanitised children's Bunyan is itself a further layer of construction.

fate: No death: a tall tale does not require one.

name: Surtr
shortDescription: The fire giant who guarded the world's edge before it existed, and will burn it down at the end.
fullDescription: Where Ymir has an origin, Surtr has none. He is already there: a fire giant standing guard at the border of Muspellheim since before the ordered cosmos began, waiting for the day he leads the sons of Muspell against the gods and burns the nine worlds to ash.
mysteryNote: The lava tube in Iceland that bears his name is still there, and still warm in places no one can explain. Locals stopped naming which places those are.
sources: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda: Gylfaginning (Iceland, c. 1220)
Poetic Edda: Völuspá, stanzas 51-53
Surtshellir archaeological surveys (Iceland)
imageAlt: Surtr, the fire giant of Muspellheim

sections.story:
Unlike Ymir, Surtr has no origin story. He is simply already there, guarding the border of Muspellheim since before the ordered cosmos began. Where Ymir's whole existence is explained in careful, sequential detail, Surtr is only ever described in terms of his function: a fixed point of destruction at the edge of the world.

At Ragnarök, he leads the sons of Muspell against the gods, kills Freyr, and sets the entire world ablaze with his flaming sword, said to shine brighter than the sun itself. He is Ymir's structural mirror: a primordial being from the opposite element, present at both the beginning and the end of the world, but where Ymir dies so the world can be built, Surtr survives to burn that same world down.

The Prose Edda's Gylfaginning describes Surtr conversationally, alongside Muspell, rather than placing him in a creation sequence. Even the text's own structure resists giving him a timeline. He is just already there, waiting.
sections.origins: Surtr's textual footprint is thin compared to Ymir's, and it is scattered across sources of different kinds and dates. The Poetic Edda's Völuspá, the oldest and most authoritative account of Ragnarök, places him at the final battle: he comes from the south bearing fire, and the sun goes black once his flame has done its work. Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda, compiled in Iceland around 1220, gives the fuller narrative context in Gylfaginning, where Surtr is introduced as already guarding Muspellheim's border, alongside a description of Muspell itself as a realm of fire predating the ordered world. Snorri is working roughly two centuries after Iceland's conversion, synthesising oral and poetic material that had already fragmented by the time it reached him.
sections.disputed: It is sometimes asked whether Gylfaginning's placement of Surtr alongside Muspell during the account of creation implies he predates Ymir. The stronger reading is that it does not: Gylfaginning is framed as a dialogue between Hár, Jafnhár and Þriði on one side and Gylfi on the other, so topics surface as they become conversationally relevant rather than in strict chronological order. Describing Surtr as already present at that point in the exchange states what exists at the time of narration, not a creation sequence. A separate, older uncertainty concerns Muspell itself: the Eddas are not fully consistent about whether it names a place, a being, or a people, and that ambiguity extends to how precisely Surtr's own role within it should be understood.

fate: Leads the sons of Muspell at Ragnarök and burns the nine worlds to ash.

scholarlyNotes.heading: A being with no origin
scholarlyNotes.body: Surtr is Ymir's structural mirror in Norse cosmology: a primordial being present at both the beginning and the end of the world. But where Ymir's origin is described in careful, sequential detail (his formation from meltwater, his death, the construction of the world from his body), Surtr has no origin story at all. He is simply already present, guarding the border of Muspellheim, and will still be standing there to burn the world down at Ragnarök. Ymir dies so the ordered world can be built; Surtr survives to end that same world.

scholarlyNotes.heading: Why the sources don't place him on a timeline
scholarlyNotes.body: It is sometimes asked whether the Prose Edda's Gylfaginning implies Surtr existed before Ymir, since he is mentioned alongside Muspell during the account of creation. The stronger reading is that this is not the case. Gylfaginning is structured as a conversation between Hár, Jafnhár, and Þriði on one side and Gylfi on the other, so topics are introduced as they become conversationally relevant, not necessarily in chronological order. Mentioning that Surtr already guards Muspellheim's border at that point in the dialogue describes what exists at the time of narration; it does not assert a creation sequence. This fits the broader pattern above: Surtr is treated as a fixed, ever-present guardian rather than a being with a beginning, and even the structure of the source text resists placing him on a timeline.

scholarlyNotes.heading: A physical trace: Surtshellir
scholarlyNotes.body: Unlike most figures in the Norse corpus, Surtr has a documented physical site associated with his name: Surtshellir, a lava tube in Iceland literally named after him. The site shows archaeological evidence of activity dating to the pagan period, with later fortification. This is unusually direct: most Norse deities exist almost entirely in text, but Surtshellir suggests active cultic association with a specific, visitable location, not simply a name applied after the fact.

name: Ispolini
shortDescription: Bulgaria's giants were God's second attempt at people. We are the third.
fullDescription: God made three attempts at people, and the dwarves were too small to survive. The ispolini were the correction.
mysteryNote: The word may be the name of a nation the Goths destroyed.
sources: Стойнев, Попов, Василева and Попов, "Исполини", Българска митология: Енциклопедичен речник, 2006
Атанас Илиев, Български предания за исполини, наречени елини, жидови и латини, Сборник за народни умотворения 3, 1890
Макс Фасмер, "исполин", Этимологический словарь русского языка, 1964 to 1973, for the Spali derivation and for Meillet's objection
Jordanes and Pliny the Elder as cited there
imageAlt: Two ispolini at a cave mouth in the Balkan uplands, autumn fog below

sections.story:
Bulgarian tradition places its giants inside a full sequence. The first people God made were dwarves, and they were too small to defend themselves from wild animals or to work the land, so they died out. To replace them God made the ispolini, deliberately as the opposite. We are the third attempt.

They stood up to three metres with enormous heads, though the regional variants differ: some give them three heads, some a single eye the size of an egg set in the forehead, some a single leg. They lived in the mountains and in caves before history and ate their meat raw. They fought dragons. Their voices carried so far that two of them could hold a conversation from separate mountaintops.

And they were frightened of blackberries. The danger was tripping over the brambles and dying, and so the ispolini made sacrifices to the plant.
sections.origins:
The word is old, and where it comes from is an argument rather than a fact. Ispolin appears meaning giant in Old Church Slavonic texts of Rus by the eleventh century. Max Vasmer derived it from the Spali, a people the Goths defeated somewhere north of the Black Sea. Jordanes records that defeat in the sixth century, and Pliny the Elder had already listed a people called Spalaei in the same region in the first.

If Vasmer is right, the Bulgarian word for a giant is the name of a nation that lost, which is the same move the folklore itself makes when it calls its giants Greeks and Latins.

He was not unopposed. Antoine Meillet argued that the initial vowel points to the word reaching Slavic through a Romance intermediary rather than directly from the ethnonym. Vasmer went through the other proposals and turned down each: a Greek Asphaloi, a Celtic Spali, a Turkic Spali, a link to Old Icelandic spjalla, and the folk reading that hears the Slavic word for field inside it.

There is a peak in the Balkan range called Ispolin.
sections.disputed: The names given to them are worth pausing on. Atanas Iliev's 1890 collection is titled, in translation, Bulgarian legends about the ispolini, called Greeks, Jews and Latins. Romanian tradition does the same thing, calling its giants jidovi, novaci and tătari. Two neighbouring traditions independently naming their prehistoric giants after historical neighbouring peoples. The giant here is not only the one who came before. He is the one who is not us, and the vocabulary gets borrowed from whoever the nearest outsider happens to be.

fate: Replaced. They were the second of three attempts, and we are the third.

name: Gargantua
shortDescription: Folk giant older than Rabelais: over four hundred French megaliths and rocks are named for him.
fullDescription: Rabelais did not invent him. The name was already in use as a nickname in 1470, and by then the countryside was full of his furniture.
mysteryNote: He left his quoit, his chair and his bowl lying about across France, and never came back for them. The Church renamed them for the devil, and the stones stayed exactly where they were.
sources: Paul Sébillot, Gargantua dans les traditions populaires, Maisonneuve, Paris, 1883
Félix Bourquelot, 1844
Henri Gaidoz
Henri Dontenville
Guy-Édouard Pillard, Le Vrai Gargantua: mythologie d'un géant, 1987
Les grandes et inestimables chroniques du grand et énorme géant Gargantua, anonymous, 1532

sections.story:
Across rural France, standing stones and strange rock formations carry his name and, more precisely, the names of his belongings. His quoit. His distaff. His skittle. His chair, his armchair, his bowl, his gravel. Sébillot, Dontenville and their successors catalogued more than four hundred such place-names, under regional variants including Grand-Tua, Grand-Tuard, Guergintua, Jergantua, Gargountoun and Gargantoua.

This is the megalith tradition at its largest recorded scale anywhere. Not a vanished race who raised the stones, but one named giant who left his things lying about.

The case that he predates literature was made by the palaeographer Félix Bourquelot in 1844 and settled by the Breton ethnologist Paul Sébillot, who in the 1880s sent a questionnaire to mythographers and local scholars across the country and published the returns in 1883. George Sand had already said it plainly: Gargantua is the work of the people, and Rabelais, like every great creator, took his material where he found it.

Then the Church took the landscape back. The places, the chasms, the rock chaoses and the standing stones called Gargantua's were rebaptised as the devil's, and the giant was set against Christian figures. The stones did not move. Only the owner's name changed.

He grew so large in the popular imagination that he absorbed the local giants around him, and anonymous or half-remembered figures across France ended up with his name attached. A few escaped: Roland in the Basque country, Hok Bras and Rannou in Lower Brittany.
sections.origins:
The literary Gargantua reaches print in 1532, in the anonymous chapbook *Les grandes et inestimables chroniques du grand et énorme géant Gargantua*, printed at Lyon, alongside Rabelais's own books of the 1530s. The folk figure is older, and it was recovered by nineteenth-century collectors rather than by literary scholarship.

Félix Bourquelot set out the case for a Gargantua preceding Rabelais in a notice of 1844, published in the Mémoires de la Société des antiquaires de France. Henri Gaidoz followed in 1868 with *Gargantua, essai de mythologie celtique*, a paper read to the Société de linguistique de Paris in the sessions of 6 and 20 June that year.

Paul Sébillot's *Gargantua dans les traditions populaires* (Maisonneuve, Paris, 1883) gathered the returns of his circulated questionnaire into the standard collection. Henri Dontenville, founder in 1950 of the Société de mythologie française, and Guy-Édouard Pillard, in *Le Vrai Gargantua* (Imago, 1987), carried the survey forward.
sections.disputed: Sébillot read the name as meaning the devourer. Later scholarship prefers something closer to the fierce or the wild. Some argue Gargantua is the residue of a Celtic god named Gargan, but there is no archaeological trace supporting that, and at least one popular etymology used to support it, reading the islet name Tombelaine as containing a Gaulish god's name, does not hold: the name derives from an older form built on *Tumba*.

fate: No death: he absorbed the local giants around him, and his stones were rebaptised as the devil's.

chain.claim: Gargantua is Rabelais's invention: the giant was made up by a sixteenth-century novelist, and everything else, including the standing stones that carry his name, is downstream of the book.
chain.verdict: The paper trail is thinner and more contested than either side of this argument usually admits, and the nineteenth-century scholars who built the case against Rabelais conceded its weakest point in their own pages.

rungs.witness: Paul Sebillot, Gargantua dans les traditions populaires, Maisonneuve, Paris
rungs.reads: Against the claim, on folklore evidence rather than documents. Sebillot describes circulating a questionnaire to mythographers and to local scholars he knew only by their publications, and printing the returns; he interrogated storytellers himself in Haute-Bretagne. He reports the name attached across France to dolmens, menhirs and large natural blocks, and a whole household of stone furniture. He states that most of the traits the tellers give are not in Rabelais, that Pantagruel, Panurge and frere Jean never appear in the oral tales, and that these traits can without rashness be regarded as older than the writings in which the name first appears. He also allows that the Grandes Chroniques and above all Rabelais's work will have spread the name of a hero who was perhaps at first only local.
rungs.evidence: /mnt/user-data/uploads/GIANTS/SOURCES/sebillot-gargantua.txt, the whole introduction, in particular lines 1145 to 1160 (the questionnaire), 1246 to 1248 and 1300 to 1307 (most traits not in Rabelais), 1308 to 1312 (older than the writings in which the name first appears), and 1400 to 1410 (the Grandes Chroniques and Rabelais spread the name). Publication data confirmed at https://archive.org/metadata/gargantuadansles00sbil: Sebillot, Paul, Gargantua dans les traditions populaires, Paris, Maisonneuve et cie., 1883.
rungs.note: The book contains its own counter-evidence. His Anjou correspondent reports that the legendary Gargantua is little known there, that the name was met once, and, in the scan's words, that the Angevin Gargantua seemed 'reste drconscrit au monde lettre' and 'ètie tout sim-plement eclos avec Rabelais' (OCR for reste circonscrit au monde lettre and etre tout simplement eclos avec Rabelais), lines 7402 to 7406. At Laval the eating proverb is judged possibly later than Rabelais, lines 7307 to 7313. Near Poitiers the Pierre de Gargantua name is contested by local antiquaries as not the popular name and in any case later than Rabelais, lines 7500 to 7533.

rungs.witness: Henri Gaidoz, Gargantua, essai de mythologie celtique, reproduced in Sebillot's introduction
rungs.reads: Against the claim: a literary work does not penetrate popular belief far enough for its hero's name to replace the older names of ancient monuments. It repeats the concession, quoting M. Baudry, that no written document naming Gargantua is found on the continent before the sixteenth century, and that a chair shown near Rouen appears in thirteenth-century charters as cathedra gygantis, the giant's chair, without the name. It then reaches for a British text, reading the Gurguntius filius nobilis illius Beleni of Giraldus Cambrensis as Gargantua, and derives the name from a root meaning to swallow, giving the sense of the devourer.
rungs.evidence: /mnt/user-data/uploads/GIANTS/SOURCES/sebillot-gargantua.txt lines 567 to 572 (Sebillot's footnote citing Revue archeologique, September 1868, pages 171 to 191), lines 582 to 611 (the passage on literary works, the Baudry objection, cathedra gygantis, and the Giraldus citation to Topographia Hibernae, II, no. 8), lines 632 to 700 (the etymology), and lines 843 to 846 (the conclusion that Gargantua is earlier than Rabelais).
rungs.note: The Giraldus text names Gurguntius, not Gargantua, and the identification is Gaidoz's own conjecture, so this rung does not deliver a pre-Rabelaisian occurrence of the name. Sebillot's footnote citation and the catalogue entry's citation do not agree; see the note field below.

rungs.witness: Gaston Paris, review in the Revue critique, quoted in Sebillot's introduction
rungs.date: 1868, pages 326 following
rungs.reads: For the claim, or at least against the case made against it. The scan reads: 'Que le ttom de Gargantua soit anterieur au livre connu sous le nom de Chroniques gargan-tuines, cela n'est pas proavi' (OCR for nom and prouve), and continues that no edition of that book earlier than 1532 exists, though copies of such popular books are rare. It adds that for a number of the sites in question the older recorded names speak simply of a giant, and that once Gargantua had become the popular type of the giant it was natural for his name to be substituted; that Gurgunt is nowhere represented as a giant and leaves no local names in England; and that a Gaulish god surviving with its mythic meaning intact would be astonishing.
rungs.evidence: /mnt/user-data/uploads/GIANTS/SOURCES/sebillot-gargantua.txt lines 883 to 899 for the quoted passage and its citation, and lines 1101 to 1108 for the Gurgunt and Gaulish god objections.
rungs.note: This is Sebillot printing his opponent at length in his own book, which is a point in the book's favour. I read it in Sebillot, not in the Revue critique.

rungs.witness: Felix Bourquelot, monograph on the popular Gargantua, quoted at length in Sebillot's introduction
rungs.date: 1844 per the catalogue entry; I could confirm only that it precedes Gaidoz's 1868 essay
rungs.reads: Argues against the claim on grounds of distribution rather than documents: the romance is a learned book full of political allusion, and could not have planted Gargantua in villages where few could read; Pantagruel, Grandgousier and Panurge left no such traces. It then concedes the decisive point. Answering the objection that no written record of the name exists before the sixteenth century, it says the tradition could have travelled by oral telling alone, and that Rabelais would be the first to write it down. It closes by saying that until a written record naming Gargantua before the sixteenth century is found, the argument will meet disbelievers.
rungs.evidence: /mnt/user-data/uploads/GIANTS/SOURCES/sebillot-gargantua.txt, uncorrected OCR of the 1883 Maisonneuve printing. Lines 308 to 311 read: 'J'avoue que si l'origine du personnage de Gargantua etait devint moi mise en question, je repondrais hardiment : Rabelais n'a point cree le type de Gargantua.' Lines 402 to 407 carry the concession about no written record before the sixteenth century; lines 560 to 565 carry the closing sentence about waiting for such a record. Bourquelot himself is corroborated at https://archive.org/download/MemoiresDeLaSocieteRoyaleDesAntiquaires17/... (volume 17, 1844), which records the admission of 'M. Felix Bourquelot' as a member and names his Histoire de Provins.
rungs.note: I could not confirm this session that the Gargantua monograph appears in that 1844 volume; Sebillot cites it by page alone, as 'Bourquelot, p. 1', which suggests a separately paginated piece. The 1844 date comes from the catalogue entry, not from anything I verified.

rungs.witness: Francois Rabelais, Gargantua
rungs.date: first printed 1534 or 1535
rungs.reads: The book the claim is about. Its date sits after the 1532 chapbook, which is the whole difficulty for the strong form of the claim.
rungs.evidence: https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargantua (fetched this session) gives the date as 1534 or 1535 and notes that Rabelais's Pantagruel of 1532 already refers to Les Grandes et inestimables chroniques du grant et enorme geant Gargantua as a book then selling in quantity. The 1868 Jacob notice fetched above likewise places the chapbook before Rabelais's Gargantua of 1535.
rungs.note: The year is not fixed in the sources I saw: 1534 and 1535 both appear. I did not open a copy of Pantagruel's prologue this session, so the cross-reference is reported, not inspected.

rungs.witness: Les grandes et inestimables cronicques du grant et enorme geant Gargantua, anonymous chapbook, Lyon
rungs.date: printed 1532; the copy I could reach is P. L. Jacob's 1868 reprint
rungs.reads: A Gargantua narrative was in print in 1532, before the Gargantua that carries Rabelais's own authorship. It does not settle the claim, because the chapbook's author is unknown and Rabelais has been proposed as that author.
rungs.evidence: archive.org item lachroniquedega00jacogoog, La chronique de Gargantua: premier texte du roman de Rabelais, ed. P. L. Jacob, 1868, fetched at https://dn760106.eu.archive.org/0/items/lachroniquedega00jacogoog/lachroniquedega00jacogoog_djvu.txt. The title page is given as Les grandes et inestimables Cronicques du grant et enorme geant Gargantua, imprime nouuellement, 1532; the notice dates the Lyon printing it knows to 1532, with a Lyon 1533 edition following, both before Rabelais's Gargantua. Separately, /mnt/user-data/uploads/GIANTS/SOURCES/sebillot-gargantua.txt line 1819 records that several authors attribute the Grandes Chroniques to Rabelais.
rungs.note: The catalogue entry is right that this book is anonymous and dated 1532, but wrong to treat it as a clean witness against Rabelais: the attribution question is open, and Sebillot himself notes it.

chain.floor: A Gargantua book was in print in 1532, before the Gargantua that Rabelais signed, so the claim in its strong form does not hold: he did not start from a blank page. What that 1532 chapbook cannot do is show how old the name was outside print, and its own authorship is unsettled, with Rabelais among the names proposed. Everything that pushes the giant back beyond the presses is nineteenth-century folklore collection and argument, and the collectors who made that case wrote down in their own pages that they had no written record of the name from before the sixteenth century.

name: Mouros
shortDescription: Builders of the megaliths of north-west Iberia: unbaptised people of the earth whose name may mean the dead.
fullDescription: They raised the standing stones in a single night, and their name may mean the dead.
mysteryNote: The stones were standing before morning. Whoever set them there went under the ground, and did not come back up.
sources: Isidoro Millán on the etymology
Galician and Asturian folk collections
the mouros are also documented under Portuguese tradition as the moura encantada

sections.story:
The mouros are found across Galicia, Asturias, León, Zamora and northern Portugal. They are described as unbaptised and pagan, and in older usage they were also called xentís, the same word the Basques use for their own megalith builders.

Every mámoa, every burial tumulus, every castro, every Roman mine, and by extension every ruin of unremembered origin is theirs. Some accounts have them raising the stones overnight. They live underground now and rarely come out, except to fetch food and at midsummer. Their money is enchanted and disappears after it is spent.

The mouras, the women, are pale from living beneath the earth or the water, blue-eyed, and guard treasure. They can take other shapes and most often choose the serpent. Some of them could fly, and carried the stones through the air themselves. Bargains made with them and then broken bring blindness, barrenness, or ruin on a family line.

The philologist Isidoro Millán derived the word not from *moro*, Moor, but from a Celtic form *mrvos*, related to the Indo-European *mr-tuos* that gives Latin *mortuus*. On that reading the people who built the old stones and live under the ground are named, quite literally, the dead. The confusion with the Moors came later, after the Muslim conquest, and runs the wrong way round.
sections.origins:
No medieval text stands behind the mouros. The tradition is oral, and reaches print only through nineteenth and twentieth century collectors.

In Portugal José Leite de Vasconcelos gathered the material from Tradições populares de Portugal (1882) onward and returned to it in Opúsculos, volume V, Etnologia (Lisbon: Imprensa Nacional, 1938). Zófimo Consiglieri Pedroso read the mouras as water spirits. Revista Lusitana, the journal Leite de Vasconcelos founded, printed Abílio Brandão's "Lendas de Mouras encantadas" in volume XIV (1911). The archaeologist Francisco Martins Sarmento treated the legends as a guide to unexcavated monuments.

Asturian versions were collected by Aurelio de Llano Roza de Ampudia in Del folklore asturiano: mitos, supersticiones, costumbres (1922). Galician versions run through the ethnographic writing of Vicente Risco and later collections such as Camiño Noia's Contos galegos de tradición oral. Alexandre Parafita's A Mitologia dos Mouros (Porto: Gailivro, 2006) is the modern Portuguese synthesis.

The Celtic etymology is a philological proposal by Isidoro Millán González-Pardo (1922 to 2002), not a folk claim.
sections.disputed: Whether the mouros are properly giants at all. Some accounts describe them as enormous, others as living much as ordinary Galician peasants did. The mouros encantados sometimes appear as giants or warriors, and a separate tradition of mourinhos describes very small underground people instead. They are best understood as the previous inhabitants rather than as a size.

fate: Went underground with the stones they raised, and stayed there.

name: Dragonja
shortDescription: Istrian giant who ploughed the Mirna into being; his kind built the hill towns.
fullDescription: He dragged a plough from the mountains to the sea. Water followed the furrow, and he named it Mirna.
mysteryNote: You can walk the whole of his day's work between breakfast and dusk, and the furrow still has water in it. Only the giants are missing.
sources: Maja Bošković-Stulli, Istarske narodne priče
Carlo De Franceschi, who recorded giant traditions around Motovun

sections.story:
Before people settled Istria, the valley of the Mirna belonged to giants. The chief among them was Dragonja, called the Ploughman, because he cut the furrow from Ćićarija down to the coast and let the river in. The border river Dragonja still carries his name.

The giants built the hill towns: Motovun, Vrh, Sovinjak, Oprtalj, Završje, Roč and Grožnjan. They were so large that each worked his own hilltop and they passed tools and building stone to one another across the valleys between. When the towns were finished there was stone left over, and rather than waste it they built one more. That is Hum, which now advertises itself as the smallest town in the world.

After the work they rested at Kotli, where the water falls in steps and where people still walk today.

Dragonja's son Gorazd is said to be in the forests of the Istrian highlands still, watching them.

Set him beside Daidarabotchi in Japan. Both are giants who made a real, named, walkable landscape by working on it while they were alive, which is the opposite of Ymir, who had to die first.
sections.origins:
This is local place-legend from the Mirna valley in central Istria, tied to named ground rather than to any medieval text: the rivers Mirna and Dragonja, the hill towns above them, the water steps at Kotli.

Nineteenth-century collecting in Istria concentrated on song. The circle around the newspaper Naša sloga gathered oral material from 1879, printed as Hrvatske narodne pjesme što se pjevaju po Istri i Kvarnerskih otocih in 1880, and Jakov Volčić recorded songs, tales and proverbs. Prose legend was the poorer relation. Carlo De Franceschi (1809 to 1893), historian of Istria and secretary of the Istrian Diet from 1861 to 1876, is the name cited for giant traditions from the Motovun district.

Systematic prose collecting came in the 1950s, when the Institut za narodnu umjetnost in Zagreb, now the Institute of Ethnology and Folklore Research, worked across the peninsula. Maja Bošković-Stulli edited the result as Istarske narodne priče (Zagreb, 1959), the first volume of the series Narodno stvaralaštvo Istre, with her introduction and commentary.

The tradition now travels largely through local tourism, which has an interest in it.
sections.disputed: The most famous Istrian giant, Veli Jože, is not folk tradition. He comes from Vladimir Nazor's novel of 1908, which draws on Istrian material but is an authored work written with a national awakening in mind. He is frequently presented as ancient. He is not.

fate: No death recorded. His son Gorazd is said to watch the Istrian highlands still.

name: Daidarabotchi
shortDescription: Japanese landscape giant: Fuji is his spoil heap, Lake Biwa the hole it came from.
fullDescription: Mount Fuji is the soil he dug out of one province. Lake Biwa is the hole he left in another.
mysteryNote: No one records a single word he said. Everything known about him is the shape he left in the ground: a lake, a mountain, and a plateau where he lay down.
sources: Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki, 8th century
Kunio Yanagita, "The Footprints of Daidarabou", Chūō Kōron, 1927, the first systematic collection of the scattered footprint legends

sections.story:
Daidarabotchi is a giant of the Kantō and Chūbu regions, known also as Deidarabotchi, Derabotchi and Daidarabō depending on where the story is told. That spread of names is itself evidence: separate local traditions arriving at the same figure.

He built Fuji from earth he scooped out of Kai Province, which is why the land around the mountain is a wide basin. When he needed more he dug again in Ōmi, and that pit filled with water and became Lake Biwa, the largest lake in Japan. He once picked up Fuji and Tsukuba to weigh them against each other and split Tsukuba's summit doing it.

Senba Lake in Ibaraki fills a single one of his footprints. The Takabocchi Plateau in Nagano is where he lay down to rest his back. The towns of Daita and Daitakubo carry his name. The earliest textual trace is in the eighth-century *Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki*, which records a giant seated on a hill eating clams from the beach and piling the shells into mounds.

Unlike almost everything else in this catalogue, he is not a threat. In Ibaraki he is remembered warmly, as a giant who shifted mountains to make life easier for the people below. He is felt through the ground he left behind rather than through any encounter.
sections.origins:
The oldest written trace is the Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki, one of the provincial gazetteers ordered by the edict of 713 and compiled in the decade after it. Its Naka district notice describes a giant on the hill at Ōkushi who reached from the hilltop to the shore for clams, the discarded shells becoming the hill itself. That hill is the Ōgushi shell mound at Shiozaki in Mito, a real Jōmon midden, protected as a national historic site since 1970. The giant there is called only ōhito, a great person. The Harima no Kuni Fudoki carries a comparable figure whose footprints filled with water and became marshes.

The name Daidarabotchi belongs to later oral tradition. Ryūtei Tanehiko noted the word in his miscellany Yōshabako, printed in 1841. The scattered local legends were first gathered as a single body of material by Yanagita Kunio in "Daidarabō no ashiato", published in Chūō Kōron in April 1927 and collected in Hitotsume Kozō sono ta (Koyama Shoten, 1934).
sections.disputed:
The etymology is unsettled. Ryūtei Tanehiko, in his miscellany Yōshabako of 1841, took the word as an insult aimed at large men, the inverse of Issun-bōshi, the one-inch boy. Yanagita derived it from Daitarō-hōshi and read the tara element as an old term of respect for a person of rank. Minakata Kumagusu took daida as a contraction of the personal name Daitarō. A separate proposal, recorded in the Nipponica encyclopedia beside Yanagita's own, links tara to tatara, the foot-bellows of iron smelting, and reads the giant as a trace of the spread of smiths.

What he originally was is also argued. Watanabe Shōgo's Nipponica article on giant legends treats him as a land-making god degraded into a comic figure as belief fell away, in company with oni and tengu. The reverse account, a yōkai tradition swelling into a giant one, also has currency.

The fudoki giants are not named Daidarabotchi. They are ōhito, great people, and the Hitachi text survives only in an abridged recension.

fate: No death: he is felt through the ground he left behind rather than through any encounter.

name: Baqbaq-Devi
shortDescription: Many-headed giants of the Georgian mountains: their strongest was outriddled, not outfought.
fullDescription: Cut off a devi's head and another grows. So the hero did not bring a sword. He brought a riddle.
mysteryNote: Cut one head and another answers. So the hero came carrying a question instead, and kept asking until the last head slept.
sources: Kartlis Tskhovreba
Dodona Kiziria, "Amirani: A Georgian Folk Hero", Folklore Forum 7, no. 7, 1974, p. 133
living oral tradition of the Georgian highlands, Christianised roughly ten centuries later than the lowlands

sections.story:
The devi are the giants of the Georgian mountains. They are many-headed, and a severed head simply grows back, which is why Georgian heroes do not win these fights by force. They win by outthinking them, or by striking at the heart.

They live underground or high in the remote Caucasus peaks, usually as a family of seven or nine brothers in a castle with their wives, their children and their hoard. When the ground shakes and a hillside tears loose, that is them.

The strongest of all of them was Baqbaq-Devi, the one the other giants deferred to. Amirani, the great Georgian culture hero, could not beat him in a straight fight and did not try. He challenged the giant to a contest of riddles instead, and used the rhythm of his own voice to put the many heads to sleep one after another. Then he stabbed him through the heart.

The word itself has travelled a long way. Georgian *devi* is kin to the Persian *div* and behind that the Zoroastrian *daeva*, the old Indo-Iranian word for a hostile spirit. The same word surfaces in South Slavic as *div* and in Albanian as *div* and *dif*. One name for a hostile giant, carried along the corridor between the Caspian and the Adriatic.

In one tale Amirani threw a devi into a ravine, and a lake formed where he fell. It is called Devi Lake. In drought the villagers still go there, throw stones into the water, and ask for rain.
sections.origins:
The devi belong to the oral tradition of the Georgian highlands rather than to any single book. The literary trace begins with *Amiran-Darejaniani*, a prose romance attributed to Mose Khoneli and usually placed in the twelfth century, though its surviving manuscripts are seventeenth and eighteenth century copies and it was not printed until Zakaria Chichinadze's edition of 1896.

Systematic collection began in the nineteenth century. Teimuraz Batonishvili published variants of the Amirani legend in 1848 and was the first to link them with Prometheus.

Marjory Wardrop's *Georgian Folk Tales* (London, David Nutt, 1894) carried devi stories into English, translated from the Aghniashvili collection *Khalkhuri Zghaprebi* (Tiflis, 1891) and from Mingrelian and Gurian collections printed at St Petersburg.

Mikheil Chikovani assembled sixty-eight recorded versions of the chained Amirani, taken down across Georgia between 1848 and 1945.
sections.disputed: Amirani, who killed Baqbaq-Devi, was himself chained to a Caucasus peak for bringing fire and metalworking to humanity, with an eagle at his liver by day and the liver regrowing by night, and a dog wearing the chain thin until smiths renew it each year. That is the Prometheus myth point for point. The Greeks placed Prometheus's rock in the Caucasus. Some scholars argue the Georgian version is older, or arose independently, which would put the famous Greek story downstream of this one. The question is open.

fate: Stabbed through the heart by Amirani, after a riddle contest put every head to sleep.

name: The Gigantes
shortDescription: Earth-born Greek race defeated by the Olympians: man-sized in the earliest art, snake-legged only later.
fullDescription: The Greek giants may not have been giants. In the earliest art they are painted as ordinary armed men.
mysteryNote: The oldest painters gave them helmets, shields and spears, and nothing stranger than that. The snakes grew later, once losing to gods seemed to require a different sort of body.
sources: Hesiod, Theogony 185
Homer, Odyssey vii.59, 206, x.120
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.6.1-2
Hyginus, Fabulae, Preface
the Gigantomachy frieze of the Pergamon Altar, 2nd century BCE

sections.story:
They were born out of violence. When Cronus castrated Ouranos, the blood fell on Gaia, and from it came three things: the Erinyes, the Meliai, and the Gigantes. Hesiod calls them strong and great, which may or may not be a statement about size.

In archaic and classical art they are shown as hoplites, man-sized and fully human, fighting in armour like anyone else. The snake legs everyone pictures do not appear until after roughly 380 BCE. The defining trait in the earliest material is strength and aggression, not stature.

Alcyoneus was immortal, but only inside his own country, so Heracles dragged him over the border and killed him there. Porphyrion attacked Heracles and Hera, and Zeus made him burn with desire for Hera instead, which was enough of a distraction to finish him. Ephialtes took an arrow in the left eye from Apollo and one in the right from Heracles.

The defeated were buried under volcanoes. Every eruption and every earthquake since is one of them moving.
sections.origins:
Hesiod's Theogony, composed around 700 BCE, gives the earliest surviving account of their birth, at line 185. Homer's Odyssey mentions them three times, as a mortal race in the far west, with no war against the Olympians attached.

There was probably an archaic epic Gigantomachia, now lost. Xenophanes, in the sixth century BCE, lists the battles of Titans, Giants and Centaurs among the stock subjects of symposium song. Pindar supplies early detail, placing the fight at Phlegra and naming Porphyrion as king.

Much of the transmission is visual rather than textual: the north frieze of the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi around 525 BCE, the east metopes of the Parthenon, the peplos woven for Athena at the Panathenaia, and the great frieze of the Pergamon Altar, raised under Eumenes II between roughly 166 and 156 BCE, excavated by Carl Humann from 1878 and now in Berlin.

The fullest connected narrative is late: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.6, compiled in the first or second century CE.
sections.disputed: The war is younger than the giants. Homer knows a savage race in the far west, ruled by Eurymedon, wiped out by their own king for their insolence toward the gods, and knows nothing whatever about a battle with the Olympians. Hesiod gives them a birth but not a war. The Gigantomachy comes later, and later writers went on to confuse the Gigantes with the Titans, an earlier and separate generation. Much of what is now assumed about them is a late assembly.

fate: Defeated by the Olympians and buried under volcanoes. Every eruption is one of them moving.

name: The Patagonian Giants
culture: European accounts of the Tehuelche and Selk'nam
height: claimed 12 to 15 feet; measured 5 ft 9 in
shortDescription: European voyage reports of a giant race in Patagonia, ended by measurement in the 1760s.
fullDescription: Fifteen feet in 1520. Four inches taller than a sailor in 1773. Nothing in Patagonia changed. Only who was doing the measuring.
mysteryNote: Magellan's men sailed home with a story that held Europe for three centuries. Two of the people in it were taken aboard, and neither reached Spain.
sources: Antonio Pigafetta, 1520s
The World Encompassed, 1628
Louis de Bougainville, 1767
the official account of the Byron voyage, 1773
imageAlt: The Patagonian Giants, european accounts of the tehuelche and selk'nam tradition

sections.story:
The first account comes from Antonio Pigafetta, who chronicled Magellan's voyage in the 1520s. Near what is now Puerto San Julián in Argentina they saw a man on the shore, naked, dancing and singing and throwing sand over his head. Magellan sent a crewman toward him with instructions to dance and sing the same way, to show they meant no harm. The man came, and was afraid, and pointed upward.

From that meeting the giants of Patagonia entered European imagination and stayed for close to three hundred years. Francis Drake's nephew repeated the claim in 1628. Later accounts put them at twelve feet, then fifteen, then higher.

The collapse came from measurement. Bougainville reported in 1767 that the tallest Patagonian he met stood five feet nine. The official account of the Byron voyage in 1773 found them roughly four inches taller than the tallest men in the crew.
