The destruction sentence is introduced with the word dizen, they say, and the fire is not free standing: it falls on the giants while they are, in Cieza's words, wrapped up in their cursed sodomy. The transcription reads: dizen, que estando todos juntos embueltos en su maldita sodomia, vino fuego del cielo temeroso y muy espantable, haziendo gran ruydo: del medio del qual salio vn angel resplandesciente con una espada tajante y muy refulgente, con la qual de un solo golpe los mato a todos, y el fuego los consumio. So the fire from heaven is there in 1553, but it arrives already fitted with a shining angel, a cutting sword, a single blow, and a sin out of Genesis.
rungs.evidence: Read twice, through two different hosts of the same article, to check the transcription against itself. https://www.redalyc.org/pdf/3210/321081234012.pdf and https://proa.ua.pt/index.php/agora/article/download/27979/20086 (Ignacio Uribe M., Pedro Cieza de Leon, los gigantes y Mercurio). Both returned the same Spanish string letter for letter and both attached the same reference, CIEZA (1553) 65v to 66v, chapter LII. Uribe's bibliography entry is CIEZA DE LEON, P. (1553), Parte primera dela chronica del Peru. Sevilla, Martin de Montesdoca. The same imprint appears independently in the bibliography of Hechler and Zurita-Altamirano at https://dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/9052563.pdf, which prints Cieza de Leon, P. de. 1553, Parte primera dela chronica del Peru. Martin de Montesdoca, Sevilla.
rungs.note: I could not open a facsimile of folios 65v to 66v this session, so the folio numbers and the spelling rest on Uribe's citation, not on my own sight of the leaf.

chain.floor: The 1553 chronicle is where the fire from heaven is documented, and it does not present it as something seen. The destruction sentence opens with dizen, they say, and the fire falls specifically on the giants' sodomy, arriving in the same breath as a shining angel and a sword that kills them all at one blow. Nothing in what survives puts a witness near the event, and the bones that kept the story alive on the peninsula were being described as animal, not human, by the 1780s.

name: Mapinguari
shortDescription: One-eyed Amazonian forest giant with a vertical mouth and a hide arrows will not enter.
fullDescription: One eye. And a mouth that opens vertically, from the nose down to the stomach.
mysteryNote: Around sixty people told the ornithologist they had seen it. Twenty years of looking produced no animal, and no end to the accounts.
sources: Luís da Câmara Cascudo, Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro and Geografia dos Mitos Brasileiros, 1976
David Oren, Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi
Florentino Ameghino
Ramón Lista

sections.story:
A great simian humanoid with long arms and heavy claws. Its hide is described as thick as a turtle's shell or an alligator's back, which is the usual explanation for why arrows and bullets are said not to enter it. Black fur in some accounts, red in most. In some regions its feet point backwards, a trait borrowed from the Curupira.

The mouth runs vertically from the nose to the stomach and is set with thousands of teeth. The single eye sits in the centre of the face.

It is also, unusually for a creature of folklore, awake in the daytime. It moves through the forest by day and rests at night in caves and hollow trunks. It is said to be able to make a person dizzy enough that the day appears to turn to night.

Domingos Parintintin, a chief of an Amazonian people, gave the practical advice: the only way to kill one is a blow to the head, and the better plan is to climb a tree and stay quiet.

Some accounts hold that a Mapinguari is what an indigenous elder eventually becomes, which it shares with the Capelobo tradition. It has also absorbed traits from other Brazilian figures it displaced in various regions, among them the Gorjala and the Pé de Garrafa.
sections.origins:
The Mapinguari is Amazonian oral tradition rather than a text. It is attested in the forests of Pará, Amazonas and Acre into the twentieth century, and is known to the Karitiana people of Brazil under other names, among them Kida harara.

Luís da Câmara Cascudo (1898 to 1986) is the collector who fixed it in print. It has an entry in his Dicionário do Folclore Brasileiro, first published in 1954, and in Geografia dos Mitos Brasileiros, first published in 1947 and reissued in 1976. Cascudo derived the name from Tupi-Guarani, roughly the thing with a crooked or backward-turned foot, and treated the figure as a composite of older Brazilian creatures.

The twentieth-century record is largely interview material. David Oren of the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi collected accounts in the Tapajós basin between the 1970s and the 1990s and published his case in 1993 and again in 2001. Transmission remains oral: hunters, rubber tappers and river communities.
sections.disputed:
This is one of the few entries in the catalogue where somebody went looking.

David Oren, an American ornithologist and former research director at the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi in Belém, spent over twenty years on it. Around a hundred people told him they had encountered the animal or heard its cry. Around sixty said they had seen it. No expedition produced one.

Oren's hypothesis, anticipated in the nineteenth century by the Argentine palaeontologist Florentino Ameghino, is that the Mapinguari preserves a memory of the ground sloths. Megatherium and Eremotherium reached six metres and were still in South America ten to twelve thousand years ago, which overlaps with the first human population of the continent.

Ameghino built the idea partly on a report from the explorer Ramón Lista, who said that while hunting in Patagonia in the 1890s he met a large unknown animal and that his bullets had no effect on it. Ameghino tied that to indigenous Patagonian descriptions of an animal whose hide arrows could barely pierce.

Whether any of this is the origin of the Mapinguari or a later scientific story laid over an older one is unresolved, and the entry does not resolve it.

fate: Not killed: said to be stopped only by a blow to the head, and better avoided from up a tree.
